Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Md SR Khoshnabish, Advocates—For the Petitioners.
Abdul Barek Chowdhury with Md Ashraful Alam and Fazlur Haque, Advocates—For the Opposite Party No. 1 in CR No. 2899 of 1998 and for Opposite Party No. 6 in CR No. 2898 of 1998.

Vs

full_judgment:
Sarif Uddin Chaklader J : These Rules by the plaintiffs are directed against the judgment and decree dated 17-5-1998 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Comilla allowing Title Appeal No. 308 of 1995 preferred by the Government and Title Appeal No. 313 of 1995 preferred by the heirs of Defendant No. 3 and thereby dismissing the suit on reversing the Judgment and decree dated 15-11-1995 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Burichang Sadar, Comilla in Title Suit No. 71 of 1995.

2. Plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit with the following prayer :-

উপরোক্ত অবস্থাধীনে ও কারণে বাদিনীর সবিনয় প্রার্থনা এই যে, (ক) নালিশী ৩য় (ক) তপছিল সম্পত্তিতে বাদীনি শান্তিভূষনদেব হইতে ১৩৬৫ বাংলা সনের ১লা আশ্বিন তারিখ হইতে খরিদমুলে মালিক ও দখলদার থাকায় নালিশী ভুমিতে বাদিনীর খরিদা ও পূর্ববর্তীক্রমে দ্বাদশবর্ষের বহু উর্দ্ধকাল ব্যাপী অন্যের বিরুদ্ধে দখল জনিত স্বত্ত্ব সাব্যস্ত তাহাতে বাদিনীর দখল স্থিরতর থাকার ডিক্রী দিতে।

3. The plaint case is that the suit land of schedules 1, 2 and 3(ka) were originally belonged to Bhogaban Chandra Deb by purchase and while he was in his raiyati title and was owner in possession, by a deed of gift dated 5th Badra, 1355 BS corresponding to 21-8-1948, transferred 52 decimals of land to his grand-sons Kanti Bhusan Deb, Narayan Chandra Deb and Shib Prashad Deb and delivered possession. On the same date, he executed another deed of gift and registered the same on 23-8-48, transferring 2nd schedule land, comprising of 44 decimals of land with structures thereon, to his other grand-sons, Shanty Bhushan Deb, Tikendra Kumar Deb, Promod Kumar Deb, and delivered possession and became title-less in respect of the suit land. Bhogaban Chandra Deb thereafter died leaving behind two sons in Palash Chandra Deb, and Suresh Chandra Deb, who inherited other lands not covered by the aforesaid deeds. Thereafter, the plaintiff by a registered deed, executed on 21st Chaitra, 1360 BS corresponding to 5-4-1954, and registered on 6-4-1954, purchased non-scheduled land from Suresh Chandra Deb and his other sons and is in possession of the said land. Shanti Bhushan Deb being eldest brother and 'Korta' of the family, by an amicable settlement in between the co-sharers, got exclusive title over 2nd schedule and being in possession of the same, executed a bainapatra on 1st Aswin, 1365 BS corresponding to 18-9-1958 in respect of 2nd schedule land with the money, delivered possession to plaintiff with the structures on the land covered by the said bainapatra and it was stipulated in the bainapatra that after obtaining clearing certificate and after giving notice of 30 days and on receiving of balance Taka 500, he would execute a register deed in respect of baina land. Shanti Bhushan Deb after giving delivery of possession of the suit land, left for India and since then, never came back to this land. The plaintiff came to know that Palash Chandra Deb later on died leaving Shanti Bhushan Deb as only son to inherit his property. Although Shanti Bhushan Deb did not register the Kabala as per the said bainapatra but the plaintiffs having been in possession for more than 12 years to the knowledge of all, acquired title over the said land by adverse possession and Government having denied title of the plaintiffs in respect of said land described in 3(ka) to the schedule and having been taken step for leasing out the said property, the cause of action of the suit arises. Plaintiffs further stated that the defendant Government tried to sell the property to some employees of the Armed forces and on 15th Bhadra, 1388 BS made a measurement of the land of the plaintiff and thereafter, the plaintiff enquired from the said employees of the Government, who did not give any satisfactory reply, filed this suit for the aforesaid relief.

4. Plaintiff having died during continuation of the suit, she was substituted by order No. 113 dated 29-3-1995. Substituted Plaintiffs thereafter filed an application for amendment of the plaint wherein it has been stated that Bhogaban Chandra Deb was possessing schedules 1 and 2 of the suit land, gave settlement of the said land to Kunjanath Bhattacharya, Provashani Dey, Soudamini Dey, Borda Kanta, Aboni Kanta Roy, Bonkim Chandra Dey, Ramesh Chandra Dey, Armada Charan Dey and Kanaklata Debi and realized rents from them and was in successive possession of schedule 3 land. In the said situation, said Bhogaban Chandra Deb transferred by a deed of gift, 52 decimals of land on 21-8-48 to Kantibhushan Deb, Narayan Chandra Deb, Shib Prashad Deb and 44 decimals of land of schedule 3 land by a deed of gift dated 21-8-1948 to Shanty Bhushan Deb, Tikendra Kumer Deb and Promod Kumer Deb and 75 decimals of land, which is situated north of the pond, to his six grand-sons, that is, Shanti Bhushan Deb, Tikendra Kumer Deb, Promod Kumer Deb, Karitibhushan Deb, Narayan Chandra Deb and Shib Prashad Deb and they were in possession of those land. Bhogaban Chandra Deb by another deed of gift on 23-8-48 transferred 31/2 decimals of land from dag No 281 with structures to defendant No. 3, Khitesh Chandra Deb and by another deed of gift, being No. 6827 of the year 1950, transferred 314 decimal of land from dag No. 282 to his daughter, Manda Sundari and delivered possession. Bhogaban Chandra Deb retains the superior interest for 1.78 decimals of land of schedule 3 and thereafter died. By a Kabala-dated 5-4-54, Suresh Chandra Deb and his 3 sons, transferred 811/2 decimals of land from schedule No. 3 to the plaintiff and delivered possession and since then the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land and SA Khatian No. 557 was correctly prepared in her name in respect of 811/2 decimals of land and was finally published. Shanti Bhushan Deb and his other two brothers, who got schedule 2 land from their father Bhogaban Chandra Deb and on his death, these three brothers got schedule 3 lands by inheritance and on amicable settlement, Shanti Bhushan Deb got 3 (ka) schedule land and his two brothers in exchange, got the lands of India. Khitesh Chandra Deb, who got 31/2 decimals of land from dag No. 281 and Manda Sundari got 3112 decimals of land from dag No. 281, by kabala deed dated 27-11-56 and 12-2-57, sold the said land to Abu Mohammad Shahnawaz, son of the plaintiff, who became the owner and possessor of the said land. After became title-less, Khitesh Chandra having fell in helpless condition, approach the plaintiff who gave him permission to possess dag No. 1925 and in such situation, Khitesh Chandra Deb wrongly recorded his name in SA Khatian. Khitesh Chandra Deb had/have no title, interest or possession in respect of said dag. Shanti Bhushan Deb through bainapatra dated 18-9-58 transferred schedule 3Ka land to the plaintiff and delivered khas possession, which includes the property requisitioned by the Government. The plaintiff by dint of said bainapatra, is in possession of half of the ponds situated in dag No. 281. Item Nos. 1, 2, 3 and schedule 3(ka) having been requisitioned by the Government, as such, the tenants of the Government are possessing the said land. The said property having been de-requisitioned and the plaintiff having been purchased the said lands and having been in possession and title over the said lands, the plaintiff acquired title of his predecessor in those lands. During SA operation, the name of Shanti Bhushan was recorded in SA Khatian No. 554 and the plaintiff having been purchased the said land from Shanti Bhushan and by paying rents, is in possession of the said land, thereby acquired good title over the suit land.

5. Government contested the suit by filing a written statement in which the Government, after taking preliminary objections as to maintainability of the suit, stated that suit Plot Nos. 159 and 160 originally belonged to Noresh Chandra Dutta who left for India before 1965 and by operation of law, this property became Enemy Property, now vested as Non-Resident Property and Khatian No. 3 having been recorded in the name of Comilla Paurashava, the plaintiff has got no right, title, interest or possession in the land of the said plots. Plaintiff's agreement is described as bogus, forged, fabricated, concocted and without any consideration. Thereafter, the Government filed additional written statement where in the Government has stated that the suit property originally belonged to Sibram Sakul, who transferred the land with other non-suited property to Bhogaban Chandra Dev and became disinterested. Bhogaban Chandra died, leaving 3 sons in Jogadish, Palash and Suresh Chandra Deb and they became owner of the suit of the land. Among them, Palash and Suresh left for India during the year 1948 and became Indian citizen and got permanent residentship. Palash Chandra Deb had 3 sons in Shanti, Tikendra and Promod. Suresh Chandra Deb also had 3 sons in Kanti, Narayan and Shib and they became owner in-possession of their respective share in the suit land. All the sons of Palash Chandra Deb and Suresh Chandra Deb are Indian resident and citizen of enemy state. The entire shares and interest of Palash Chandra Deb and Suresh Chandra Deb vested in the Government on and from 3-12-65 vide GO No. 1199 dated 3-12-65. Buildings over the suit lands, were requisitioned in Requisition Case No. 291 of 1948 and were taken over from Bhogaban Chandra Deb. This property also de-requisitioned in favour of the Government and subsequently leased out to the allottees in VP Cases Nos. 32-33/86 and the lessees are in possession and Government realized lease money from them. The suit land is Enemy property and now vested in the Government. The story of title by adverse possession is bogus and the impugned bainapatra is false and denied by this defendant.

6. Defendant No. 3 contested the suit by filing a written statement wherein he denied the plaint case line by line and the specific case of this defendant is that Bhogaban Chandra Deb became owner in possession of the suit land of schedules 1 and 2 by purchase. Bhogaban had 3 sons, Jogadish Chandra Deb, Palash Chandra Deb and Suresh Chandra Deb. Amongst them Jogadish was eldest and while Bhagaban Chandra Deb became old, Jogadish looked after the properties with other house hold affairs of Bhogaban Chandra Deb. Jogadish died leaving son, defendant No. 3. After the death of Jogadish, his two other brothers, Palash Chandra Deb and Suresh Chandra Deb took management to the property and defendant No. 3 also helped Palash Chandra and Suresh Chandra in all the business of the family which was done in the name of Palash Chandra Deb and Suresh Chandra Deb. To enrich the business of the family i.e. contractor, timber /furniture and to enrich the income of the family, Palash Chandra and Suresh Chandra and defendant No. 3 went to Calcutta and Agartala of India and started business there and by income of the business, they purchased land at Beleghata in Calcutta and another at Jogendra Nagar at Agartala and constructed two houses for their business purpose. They used to live in certain portion of those two houses and let out other portions. As such, the business of this defendant became loosing concern and Palash Deb and Suresh Chandra Deb took loan from Tripura National Bank which also did not made any good to their business and Bank issued notice for repayment of the loan. At that time, Bhogaban Chandra Deb was in the verge of death and on the assumption of his demise, Boghaban Chandra Deb, on the apprehension that the property of them might be put into auction, made a deed of gift on 23-8-48 in favour of Shanti Bhusan Deb, Tikendra Kumar Deb, Promad Kumer Deb, Tikendra Kumer Deb, Promad Kumer Deb, Kantibhusan Deb, Narayan Chandra Deb and Shib Prashad Deb in respect of schedules 1 and 2 to the suit land, but in fact, Bhagaban Chandra Deb did not made any gift to his grandsons, it was merely a paper transaction and there was no such occasion for the gift. Bhogaban Chandra Deb only to protect the property, made the said gift and after the said gift, Bhogaban Chandra died. At the time of aforesaid deed of gift, all the grandsons of Bhogaban Chandra Deb were minor and Bhogaban Chandra did not delivere possession to those grandsons and no one on behalf of the said sons, took delivery of possession of the gifted land. And by these gifts, grandsons of Bhogaban Chandra Deb did not acquire any title over schedule 1 and 2 land. After the death of Bhogaban Chandra Deb, the property of Palash Chandra Deb was put into auction in Certificate Case No. 3/48-49 and was sold in auction. The Government in Requisition Case No. 291 of 1948 requisitioned the structure from Bhogaban Chandra Deb on 4-9-48. After the death of Bhogaban Chandra Deb, as per Daibhaga Law of inheritance, Palash Chandra Deb, Suresh Chandra Deb and defendant No. 3 inherited the suit land and possessed schedule 1 and 2 lands in ejmali for some time and thereafter, by an amicable partition, this defendant No. 3 got the land of Comilla and also schedule Nos. 1 and 2 in possession of the same. Palash Chandra and Suresh Chandra having been decided to live in India as per amicable partition, the house of Beleghata of Calcutta was allocated to Palash Chandra Deb and the house of Jogendra Nagar at Agartala was allocated to Suresh Chandra Deb where they lived with their wives, sons and daughter and had possessed the same. Palash Chandra died in Calcutta and after his death, his sons, Shantibhusan Deb, Tikendra Kumer Deb and Promad Kumer Deb are living in Calcutta and the heirs of Suresh Chandra Deb i.e. Kantibhushan Deb, Narayan Chandra Deb and Shib Prashad Deb are living in Agartala. The defendant No. 3 having got the lands and property of Comilla with the schedule lands of the suit properties, as per the said amicable partition, are living in the said properties with his wife, sons and daughters for more than 12 years and having let out the structures and realizing rents, possessing the suit lands. Defendant No. 3 living in the said land from the time of his grand-father, Bhoban Chandra Deb. Suresh Chandra Deb or his sons did not transfer schedule 1 land by deed dated 5-4-54, registered on 6-4-54 and never delivered possession of the said schedule 1 land as sons of Suresh or Suresh did not have such right to transfer. Ali Ahmed Majumder, husband of the plaintiff was Officer-in-Charge of the Thana, was a greedy person, who was a monthly ejectable tenants in schedule 1 land and by practicing fraud with the scribe and the witnesses, made the said deed. He did not take any permission for vendors, who were minors at the time of registration of the sale deed. None of the witnesses of this deed was a man of the same locality and by this deed the plaintiff acquired no title over schedule 1 land. Ali Ahmed Majumder had a bad reputation and, as such, the local people killed him. Shantibhusan did not execute the bainapatra on 18-9-58 nor did he receive Taka 4,500 out of Taka 5,000 as claimed on 18-9-58 as Shantibhusan Deb left for India before 18-9-58 and became resident of Beleghata in Calcutta. In fact, there was no agreement or any talk of sale in between plaintiff and Shantibhusan, the said bainapatra is forged, fabricated, illegal and concocted document. The plaintiff and her husband by forgoing the signatures of this defendant, created the saf-kabala deed dated 7-2-58 which was registered by false personification and this being detected, Ali Ahmed returned this false deed to this defendant No. 3. During liberation war, the plaintiff became care taker of 2nd schedule land by a peace committee and after liberation of the country, freedom fighters recovered the said property from the plaintiff and gave it to this defendant. The plaintiff never purchased the said land and was never in possession. The SA khatian in respect of recording the name of the plaintiff was prepared in collaboration with the employees of the settlement office. This defendant further stated that the still land was never vested and non-resident property and it was wrongly been declared as enemy property.

7. Defendant Nos. 3Ka to 3uma, heirs of defendant No. 3 also contested the suit. They denied the plaint case and in their lengthy written statements, they in fact re-narrated the case of defendant No. 3 with some improvement.

8. Trial Court on the pleading of the parties, framed 7 issues and on consideration of the depositions of 5 PWs, DW 1, 2, 3, 4 who were examined for defendant No. 3 and DWs 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 who were examined on behalf of Government and on consideration of a number of Exhibits filed by the plaintiff, defendant No. 3 and Government, decreed the suit. The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the evidences on record found the impugned bainapatra as genuine and the plaintiffs are successful in establishing their title and possession over the suit land. Two appeals were preferred, Defendant No. 3 preferred Title Appeal No. 313 of 1995 and Defendant No. 1, Government, preferred Title Appeal No. 308 of 1995 and both appeals on transfer, were heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Comilla and by the impunged Judgment and decree dated 17-5-1998 the learned Judge allowed both the appeals and dismissed the suit.

9. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff, submits that the plaintiff filed the instant suit for declaration of title in respect of the land covered by Exhibit 7 by adverse possession and he having been proved her possession by adducing independent witnesses as well as by documentary evidences that she is in possession of the suit land for over statutory period of limitation and thereby acquired good title against her vendor, the Court of appeal below taken a wrong view of the plaintiffs case and was fallen into error of law and fact in disbelieving the bainapatra holding the same to be a spurious document and dismissed the suit. He further submits that by Exhibit 3 series, Bhogaban Chandra Deb divested his title in favour of his grandsons and there being no contrary evidence on record, the Court of appeal below was in error of law in holding that plaintiff's entry to the suit land on the basis of those documents having not been proved, as such, she acquired no title either by purchase or by adverse possession over the suit land. Mr Khondker further submits that the Court of appeal below was not justified in holding Khitesh Chandra lived in the suit land on per-missive possession as it admitted position that Khitesh Chandra, Palash Chandra and Suresh Chandra were living in India for their business purpose after divesting their interest over the suit land. He further submits that the Court of appeal below on misreading of the evidence on record, particularly Exhibit 7, and disbelieved the plaintiff's witnesses without any basis, passed the impugned judgment which is therefore not sustainable in law.

10. Mr Md Ashraful Alam, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of defendant No. 3ka-3uma opposite parties submits that the Court of appeal below committed no illegality in disbelieving Exhibit 7, the bainapatra as none of the witnesses of the bainapatra came forward to depose, as such, although these document is of 30 years old but the plaintiff would not get the benefit of section 90 of the Evidence Act. He further submits that Exhibit 17 does not tally with the bainapatra, Exhibit 7, and without any explanation as to the interpolation found in bainapatra, Exhibit 7, the Court of appeal below committed no illegality in not putting any reliance on this Exhibit 7. The learned Advocate on referring to certain portions of the judgment, that is pages 67 to 71 of the certified copy of the judgment annexed with CR No. 2899 of 1998 and also pages 66, 67, 68 and 80, submits that the Court of appeal below committed no illegality in holding that the plaintiff fails to prove his exclusive possession over the suit land as the Court of appeal below in these pages of the judgment conclusively held that the plaintiff has no possession over the suit land. He further submits that all the witnesses of the plaintiff do not say properly as to the entry of the plaintiff in the suit land and that being so, the Court of appeal below committed no illegality in disbelieving the plaint case.

11. Mr Fazlul Hoque, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Government, submits that the suit land stands in the name of the Government before partition of 1947 and thereafter as enemy property from 1948 as the Government requisitioned the property from Bhogaban Chandra and thereafter, having found Suresh Chandra and Plash Chandra living India, release the property in favour of Government as the property by this time became abandoned property and the plaintiff having failed to prove his possession at no point of time, the acquisition of title by adverse possession does not arise. Mr Fazlul Hoque, the learned Advocate further submits that Government does not claim the land of Khitesh Chandra as enemy property.

12. The submissions of the learned Advocates of the parties led me to consider whether Exhibit 7 is a genuine document, whether plaintiff proves adverse possession against her vendor and whether defendant No. 3 is a permissive possessor from plaintiff. The entire onus lies upon plaintiff. If the plaintiff has been able to prove she acquired title by adverse possession against her vendor, then the property cannot be declared to be a vested property in either form, that is, as enemy or abandoned property, as the plaintiff in that case, being admittedly a Bangladeshi, got title of the property and therefore, this property cannot be declared to be a vested and non-resident property. The plaintiff has also a little onus to prove whether defendant No. 3 was her licensee to live on the suit property and in that case, defendant No. 3 has a onus to prove that he by his own right, possess the suit land. Before going to the merit of the case, at the outset it is to be pointed out defendant Nos. 3ka to 3uma are the sons of defendant No. 3. Defendant No. 3 filed written statement on 23-2=84 and defendant Nos. 3ka to 3uma filed written statement on 5-9-93. Defendant Nos. 3ka to 3uma are the sons of Khitesh Chandra Deb. I do not understand how defendant Nos. 3ka to 3uma filed written statement in front of the written statement of defendant No 3. The plaint, as it appears, was filed, at first against Government of Bangladesh. Thereafter by an amendment dated 8-11-83, Assistant Custodian of Vested Property was added and thereafter by a further amendment by order No. 27 dated 21-12-83, defendant No. 3 Khitesh Chandra Deb was added. I will consider later on whether two written statements could be filed on behalf of same defendant under law.

<u>13. Plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of the title by adverse possession against her vendor. It is the case of the plaintiff that she entered into possession through a bainama executed by the admitted owner, Bhogaban Chandra in 1958 and since then she is in possession up to 1981 when she filed the suit and thereby acquired title over the suit land by adverse possession. What is adverse possession? It is such a possessions which extinguish actual owner's title. To make a possession adverse, there must be an entry under a colour of right claiming title hostile to the true owner and the world and this must be followed by possession and appropriation of the premises to the occupants use done openly. Title by adverse possession becomes complete only when the possession continues uninterruptedly for the full statutory period. This possession means actual physical possession. Thus question of adverse possession is a mixed question, at first fact, then law. The claimant must prove such possession is over and without concealment and be adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent and implies it commences in wrong and is maintained against right. Such possession of the claimant must be uninterrupted at least for 12 years. If it is proved claimant loses possession even for a day before completion of 12 years, then he had no right to claim title by adverse possession. Aforesaid discussions led me to hold title by adverse possession is an act of the claimant by which possessor possess the property in question hostile under a claim of title, actually, openly, uninterruptedly notorious, exclusively and continuously for a period of 12 years and if the claimant prove so, it confers an indefeasible title upon the possessor. The quality and extension of right acquired by adverse possession always depends upon the claim accompanying it and upon the nature of animus possedendi. The question whether possession is adverse or not is always a question of one's own intention to hold adversely and knowledge of such intention must be brought home to be real owner so as to extinguish his title. Keeping this view in mind I am now consider whether plaintiff could prove the case of title by adverse possession.</u>

14. To consider the plaint case as to acquisition of title by adverse possession I am now to consider the entry of plaintiff into the suit property, which the plaintiffs claimed through Exhibit 7. The trial Court believed this Exhibit and taken as it to be basis or foundation of plaintiff's case. The appellate Court on the other hand disbelieved this Exhibit on the ground that there being some interpolations in it and also finds this Exhibit 7 is a forged, fraudulent, consideration less and inoperative document. From perusal of Exhibit 7, 1 find it has been written in two pages, one page is of stamp paper of 1Rs 8 Annas and another one is a cartridge paper. The Court of appeal below disbelieved it finding some interpolations in respect of date mentioned according to English calendar. The date of execution was 18-9-58. The Court of appeal below on consideration of Exbt. 7 found interpolation in figure "9" to "59" which is turned in to "8" of "58" But the Court of appeal below failed to consider the Bengali date was no interpolated from 1st Aswin 1365 BS and it remained in fact. It can be said to be a forged document if both the Bengali date as well as corresponding English date been interpolated. But in the instant case, the Court of appeal below over looked the Bengali date which has not been altered and it is found to be correct as corresponding year of 1365 BS would be 1958 AD. I do not find how the learned Judge has taken the view that only in changing the figure '8' the entire document could be taken as to be a forged document when the Bengali date remains unaltered. It is a correction to the year according to English calendar. Learned Judge also took exception of the stamp paper, which is dated 3-3-56 i.e. much earlier to the date of execution. On a perusal of Exhibit 7, I find it was purchased on 3-3-56 and Exhibit 7 was executed on 18-9-58. It is not so late which could make this Exhibit 7 as questionable. It is not the case of the defendants that the stamp paper was of subsequent date. Nor it is their case that the agreement was not written on the date mentioned therein. A question was posted by the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 3 that the stamp paper was purchased in the name of Nurul Islam, who is not a party to Exhibit 7. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, on the other hand submits Nurul Islam is the full brother of the plaintiff. When defendant No. 3 did not challenge the execution or tried to prove this document as forged by sending it to the expert, because onus lies upon him to disprove the signature appeared in Exhibit 7, are not of him, this fact i.e. stamp was purchased on the name of some other person, in my opinion, is not a matter of so much importance. Learned Judge did not consider the recital and contents of Exhibit 7 but consider only interpolation of figure '8' of 58, and found this document carriage no value as it is forged one. Bengali date of Exhibit 7 had not been changed or no interpolation was made thereon and without considering the corresponding Bengali year of 1958 AD which is Bengali 1365, learned Additional District Judge fallen into error of law in holding this bainapatra is a forged document which finding I hold arrived purely on misreading and non-reading of Exhibit 7.

15. On the question of proving Exhibit 7 the learned Judge held that since none of the witnesses to Exhibit 7 examined this Exhibit 7 remains not proved. It is to be borne in mind that the suit was filed on 15-9-1981. I find 8 witnesses signed this Exhibit-7. Plaintiff examined PW 3 Md Haroon-or-Rashid, son of late Abdur Rahman and PW 5 Fakhrul Huq, son of late Abdul Gafur who proved the signatures of their fathers in Exhibit 7 as witnesses. The Court of appeal below without any basis arrived at a finding that these two witnesses, that is PW 3 and 5 are not competent witnesses to prove the signatures of their late father in Exhibit 7. I do not understand from what analogy the learned Judge held so. Who would be the better witness to prove the signatures of father excepting his sons? The entire judgment of the Court of Appeal below centre round this finding i.e. genuinely of Exhibit 7. From the forgoing discussions I am of the opinion the learned Judge totally on misreading and non-reading of exhibt-7 and depositions of PW 3 and 5 held Exhibt-7 as forged which is neither legal nor proper and I hold this Exhibit-7 is a genuine document to be consider as a document of title.

16. The Court of Appeal below on the question of possession found plaintiff witnesses fails to prove exclusive possession of the plaintiff as they could not say as to the quantum of land involve in the suit. The plain-tiff in order to prove possession, filed rent receipts, Exhibit 9 series, ranging from 1365 to 1401 BS. The plaintiff also filed Exhibit 10 series, rent receipts of Comilla Paurashava, ranging from 1978-79 up to 1991-1992. The plaintiff also produced Exhibit 11, the order sheet of IT Case No.3 of 1948-49, and the order dated 18-11-50. From perusal of this Exhibit 11, I find the order contends that Bhogaban Chandra purchased CS plot Nos. 280, 281, 282 and 285 with an area of 3.83 acres by registered deed No. 2466 dated 22-6-36, recorded in Khatian No. 158 of Mouza Kandirpar and plot Nos. 159 and 160 with an area of 0.52 acres of land purchased from Abonikanta Roy. It further contends that Bhogaban Chandra gifted the said land to his grandsons. Shantibhusan Deb and 5 others vide deed No. 6797 registered on 23-8-48 and deed No. 6798 registered on 23-8-48. From this order I further find municipal papers submitted proved the area was divided into holding Nos. 295, 296, 297, and 298. I also find from this order Palash Chandra Deb got no title and interest of the said property at Thakurpara. The plaintiff also filed the order of EP Case No. 52 of 1967-68 and EPL Case No. 119 of 1970-71. Exhibit 13 is the notice of Comilla Paurashava served upon the plaintiff wherein it has been stated that:—

“মহল্লাস্থিত আপনার দখলীয় পুকুরে কচুরীপানা জমিয়াছে।”

SA Khatian No. 554 is Exhibit Kha, PRR Khatian No. 1156/1 is Exhibit 14 and Exhibit 16 is the Assessment list of the Comilla Municipality wherein description of the structures along with the area of the land has been given. The learned Additional District Judge did not consider these documents. He disbelieved Exhibits 9 and 10 on the ground that these are not in consistent with the oral evidence adduced by the plaintiff. Plaintiff examined PW2 Md Alam Majumder, who in his deposition, stated that :— “তারা বরাবরই এখানে বাস করে। কেমন করে বাস করে জানি না।”

This witness was not cross examined by defendant PW4 in his deposition stated:—

“নালিশী জমি বাদীরা দখল করে। শম্ভ্যাংরা নালিশী জমিতে আছে ভাড়াটিয়া হিসাবে।”

This witness was cross-examined by defendant Nos. 3ka to 3uma and in his cross-stated:— 	“ঘর ও দালানে বাদীর ভাড়াটিয়ারা আছে।”

PW5 in his deposition stated that:-

“নালিশী জমিতে ২ টি টিনের ঘর, ১ টি পায়খানা, ১ টি ভগ্ন দোতলা দালান, ১টি পাকের ঘর আছে। ক্ষীতিশ বাবু অনুমতি নিয়াছেন আম্মা থেকে। বায়না পত্রের পর থেকেই ইং ১৯৫৮ ইং শেষের দিকে অনুমতি দিয়াছেন। আমি তখন নাবালক ছিলাম। অনুমতি দেবার কোন দালিলিক প্রমান নেই। মৌখিক সাক্ষী ছিল। আমি সেরকম সাক্ষী মানিনি।”

The Court of appeal below take this statement and hold since this witness was a minor, may be at the age of 5/6 years, as such, no understandable capacity to understand what is permissive possession was grown in him and disbelieved the plaintiffs case and possession and also permissive possession on a wrong presumption. It is found that PW1 was 5/6 years old when permissive possession was given to defendant No. 3. It is not the case of defendant No. 3 that PW 1 was not living in the suit property such continuous living with his mother make him understand what is meant and understand by permissive possession. I will consider the case of permissive possession, the case of defendant No. 3 later on but at first the question as to whether plaintiff has been able to prove his possession and title by adverse possession is to be consider. From the aforesaid discussions of the Exhibits as well as depositions, the plaintiff at last could prove she is in possession of the suit land from 1958. The learned Advocate for the Government gave much emphasis on Exhibits 'ja', and 'jha' the proceedings of EP Case No. 52 of 1967-68 and EPL Case No. 119 of 1970-71, which are Exhibits relating to leasing of case land to different lessee. I find the first date appears therein is 24-3-67. I find Sufia Akter raised objections although. From the order dated 31-7-71 it appears the objection raised by Sufia Akter, the plaintiff, was rejected. It the body of the order the Superintendent Enemy Property (L&B) Comilla found all the owners of the above plots, namely Shantibhusan Deb, Tikendra Kumer Deb and Promod Deb, sons of Palash Chandra Deb and Khitesh Bhusan Deb, Narayan Deb and Shib Dulal Deb, who got the suit property through registered deed of gift dated 23.8.48, left the country and in absence of them, Begum Sufia Akhter manage the plots and manage to record the plots in her name. This fact goes to show the possession of plaintiff Learned Advocate for the Government while arguing the case, submits Government do not claim the land of Khitesh Chandra Deb as not enemy property. Although Exhibits 'ja' and lha' does not show Khitesh Chandra as the owner of the land. From Exhibit 'Jha', I find Sufia Akhter, the plaintiff although contested case by filing objection. Before 1968 there is no record on the part of the Government, excepting requisition proceeding, to prove Government ever tried to settle this land as Enemy Property or to that effect, in the alternative, as abandoned property. Requisition in the instant case is not for acquisition. Requisition means ownership of the property is retained by the owner. If it is the case of the Government that Government for acquisition of the property, requisitioned those lands from its owner Bhogaban Chandra Deb, then the Government case have at least a cripple structure. From Exhibit 17 series it appears Government de-requisitioned some non suited property in favour of Sufia Akhter at the appellate stage. The plaintiff filed applications (Exhibits 17 to 21) and Exhibit 17 speaks Government release the property of Requisition Case No. 291 of 1948 to Begum Sufia Akhter and it appears from Memorandum No. 2188 dated Comilla the 29-7-1954, wherein it has been stated, in the way of modification of the office order, "she is informed that the schedule shown in the above order has been replaced" and it is seen from this memorandum that possession of the house was made over to her on 7-7-54. Exhibit 18 is the receipt from Comilla Paurashava for payment of rent for the year of 1982-83. Exhibit 19 series and Exhibit 20 series shows plaintiffs paying taxes in respect of holding No. 471/433 and Exhibit 21 i.e. khatian No. 557 Stands in the name of Sufia Akhter. Although these are not directly relating to the suit plot No. 1925 but it goes to show remaining part of .the suit land requisitioned by the Government was released in favour of the plaintiff. Although the Government took up a point that its bharatia/ tenants are on the suit land. But if it is found the plaintiffs have acquired title against his vendor by adverse possession, the Government in no way could take over this property in either form, as enemy property or abandoned property. Since I have already found Exhibit 7 is a legal document and since I have found plaintiffs through different Exhibits as well as depositions and also from Exhibit Ja and Jha series prove her possession, I find plaintiff's case as to adverse possession in absence of any contrary evidence adduced by the defendants has been established because from the forgoing discussion it is seen the plaintiff's starting point of possession is from 1958 and suit having been filed on 15-9-1981, plaintiff possession is more than 12 years and these being no evidence, either oral or documentary to speak at any point of time plaintiff loses her possession, this possession in sufficient to confer her title by adverse possession against her vender.

17. One question may be posted i.e. since the Government tenants are in the suit land whether consequential relief is required to be prayed for or not. In the case reported in 43 DLR 109 it has been held that if it is declared by the Court that the property is not an abandoned property, the Government will have no reason to possess the same and will be under an obligation restore possession to the plaintiff and no prayer for recovery of possession as consequential relief is necessary. Since this judgment still governed this field. I find the suit as framed is maintainable.

18. Now turning to the question permissive possession. There are two sets of written statements filed by defendant No. 3 and defendant Nos. 3 ka to 3uma. The trial Court found that defendant No. 3 is in permissive possession. I have already pointed out in this suit defendant No. 3 filed written statement and defendant Nos. 3ka to 3uma filed another written statement. These defendant Nos. 3ka to 3 uma are the sons of defendant No. 3 late Khitesh Chandra Deb who is appellant of Title Appeal No. 308 of 1995. Order VIII of the Code of Civil Procedure speaks for filing of single written statement by any party. Two written statements on behalf of the same party cannot be considered under law as order VIII of the Code of Civil Procedure does not permit so. It is very curious to finch both the written statements are on record When two written statements are filed or behalf of same party then the proper course open to the Court is not to consider any one o them because it is not possible to find which one of these two written statements speaks the true defense case. Order VIII of the Code of Civil Procedure permits for filing additional written statement or with permission of the Court, better statement but it does not permit to file separate written statement on behalf of same defendant. I do not understand how defendant Nos. 3ka to 3uma filed written statement in this suit. This written statement filed by defendant Nos. 3ka to 3uma in fact to improve the written statement filed by defendant No. 3. Law in such situation speaks for non-consideration of both these written statements. But since appellate Court passed a judgment in favour of defendant No. 3 or to that effect, defendant Nos. 3ka to 3uma I take up the written statement filed by the defendant No. 3 for consideration. This written statement nowhere speaks how defendant No. 3 entered into the suit land. The relevant portion of this written statement I quoted so that the case of the defendant No. 3 could be understand. In Paragraph 16 of the written statement is as follows;

“উক্ত প্রকারে ব্যবসা চলিতে থাকাবস্থায় পলাশ চন্দ্রদেব, পরেশ চন্দ্র দেব ও উত্তরকারী বিবাদী ব্যবসা বৃদ্ধি প্রত্যাশায় তৎকালীন অবিভক্ত ভারতের কলিকাতা ও আগরতলায় গিয়া ব্যবসা শুরু করেন।”

That means it is sometime before 1947. Thereafter this written statement is silent as to when this defendant No. 3 entered into the suit land. The relevant portion as to re-enter of defendant No. 3 into the suit land is at paragraph 18 of the written statement wherein it is written as—

“ভগবান চন্দ্র দেব অপরাপর সম্পত্তিসহ  ১ম ও ২য় তফছিলের সম্পত্তিতে মালিক দখলদার থাকাবস্থায় পলাশ চন্দ্র দেব ও সুরেশ চন্দ্র দেবকে দুই পুত্র এবং উত্তরাধিকারী ৩ নং বিবাদীকে  মৃত পুত্রের পুত্র অর্থাৎ পৌত্র ওয়ারিশ বিদ্যমানে পরলোকবাসী হইলে উত্তরকারী বিবাদী হিন্দু দায়ভাগ আইনের বিধানমতে ভগবান চন্দ্রদেবের ত্যাজ্য বিত্তে ওয়ারিশ সুত্রে তুল্যাংশে মালিক দখলদার হয় ও বিদ্যমান আছে। অতঃপর সকল শরীকগণ কিছুকাল এজমালিতে ও একান্তে থাকার পর শরীকান মধ্যে পারিবারিক আপোষ সংস্থামতে অপরাপর সমুদয় বিত্ত সম্পত্তি বিভাগ বন্টন হইলে উত্তরকারী ৩ নং বিবাদী কুমিল্লাস্থিত অন্যান্য সম্পত্তিসহ ১ম ও ২য় তফছিলের সম্পত্তি আপোষকালীন একক প্রাপ্ত হইয়া তাহাতে মালিক দখলদার হয় ও বিদ্যমান আছে।”

Then on the same paragraph this defendant stated-

উক্ত প্রকারে উত্তরকারী ৩ নং বিবাদী কুমিল্লাস্থিত অপরাপর সম্পত্তি ও নালিশী ২য় তপছিলের সম্পত্তি ওয়ারিশ সুত্রে আপোষ বন্টনে একক প্রাপ্ত হইয়া তাহাতে নিজ স্বত্ত্ব প্রচারে অন্যের স্বত্ত্ব অস্বীকারে অন্যের বিরুদ্ধে দখল জনিত স্বত্ত্বে মালিক দখলদার হয় ও বিদ্যমান আছে এবং তদান্তরে বসত বাড়ীতে স্ত্রী পুত্র কন্যাদি নিয়া দ্বাদশ বৎসরের বহু উর্দ্ধকাল ব্যাপী বসবাস করিয়া এবং কতেক অংশের দালান কোঠা ও গৃহাদি ভাড়া দিয়া ভাড়ার টাকা নিয়মিতভাবে গ্রহণ করিয়া আসিতেছে।

This defendant further has written:—

“এখানে প্রকাশ থাকে যে, শরীকান মধ্যে বিষয় সম্পত্তি আপোষ বন্টন হওয়ার পর পলাশ চন্দ্রদেব ও সুরেশ চন্দ্র দেব  তাহাদের পিতা ভগবান চন্দ্র দেবের ২৩-৫-৫৮ ইং তারিখের দানপত্র নামধেয় মুল দলিল উত্তরকারী বিবাদীকে বুঝাইয়া দিয়া যায় এবং বর্তমানে ঐ মূল দলিল উত্তরকারী বিবাদীর নিকট আছে।”

Thereafter, this defendant did not state anything as to how and when he got into possession of the suit land as of his own right. Defendant No. 3ga examined himself as DW 1, for defendant No. 3 and in his deposition, I find he produced certified copy of Requisition Case No. 291 of 1948 as Exhibit Ka, the deed of gift dated 23-8-48 as Exhibit Kha, the deed of husband of plaintiff as Exhibit Ga, the information slip as Exhibit Gha in respect of Khatian No. 554 and Exhibit Uma in respect of Khatian No. 555. I find the case of this defendant that he possessed the suit land through tenants have not been supported by any of these documents. From the records, I find Khitesh fails to prove his title over the suit land by producing any documents as Khitesh Chandra did not possess any document after executing Exhibit 7 dated 18-9-1958 by which his title has been evaporated. Through written statement he did not specify when he re-enter into the suit land, as such, he cannot be considered to be better than permissive possessor. The appellate Court reversed the finding of the trial Court on the findings plaintiff No. 1 was minor boy of merely 5 years could not understand what is meant by permissive possession. It is not denied PW 1. At that time, it taken to be true, a mere child of 5 years of age but it is not the case of defendant that her mother, that is plaintiff, at no point of time during his long association disclosed about the status of defendant No. 3 before his as the suit was filed on 15-9-1981 and by this time PW 1 understand in what status defendant No. 3 possessed a fraction of the suit land. Moreover, the understandings of a child are not discarded but their Such understanding should be taken into consideration with much caution. PW 1 in 1958 was a boy of 5 years and the suit was filed in 1981 and by this time he was major enough to understand what is meant by permissive possession. I find the judgment of the Court of appeal below on the aforesaid discussions, needs to be interfered. I find substance in these rules.

19. In the result, both rules are made absolute without any order as to costs. The Judgment and decree dated 17-5-1998 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court Comilla, in Title Appeal No. 305 of 1995 and Title Appeal No. 313 of 1995 are set aside Title Suit No. 71 of 1995 is decreed.
